metadata.source_title: Evolution and Selection of Quantitative Traits

blocks.content: With Holm's method, we stop once we fail to reject a hypothesis. An improvement on this approach is the Simes-Hochberg correction (Simes 1986; Hochberg 1988), which effectively starts backward, working with the largest p values first.
(i) If $ p(n) $, then all hypothesis are rejected.
(ii) If not, $ H(n) $ cannot be rejected, and we next examine $ H(n-1) $.
(iii) If $ p(n-1) /2 $, then all $ H(i) $ for $ i n-1 $ are rejected.
(iv) If not, $ H(n-1) $ cannot be rejected, and we compare $ p(n-2) $ with $ /3 $.
(v) In general, if $ p(n - i) /(n - i + 1) $, then all $ H(i) $ for $ i n - i $ are rejected.

While the Simes-Hochberg approach is more powerful than that of Holm's (see Example A4.4), it is only strictly applicable when the group of tests being jointly considered are independent, whereas Holm's approach does not have this restriction. Hence, the general strategy is to use Holm's method if one is concerned about potential dependencies between tests, and the Simes-Hochberg's method if the tests are independent.
